overview: Bosnia and Herzegovina emerged from Yugoslavia’s dissolution and joined the United Nations in 1992. The imported map begins in 1994, during a devastating war, and continues into peace and rebuilding. It shows the country’s outer outline, not the wartime lines of control or the separate layers of its later government.

periods.title: Independence and war
periods.summary: The new international state endured war before the Dayton settlement.

periods.title: Peace and reconstruction
periods.summary: The peace agreement preserved Bosnia and Herzegovina while setting out a new constitutional structure.

items.text: Woodcarvers in Konjic make furniture, decorated interiors and smaller objects with recognisable hand-cut motifs. The work can turn a functional household piece into something passed down within a family. The craft remains both paid work and a hobby.

Young woodcarvers learn on the job in practising workshops and from older relatives. Family-run businesses help train apprentices and maintain the skills. Knowing which tool to use and how to guide it cannot be passed on by a finished chair alone.

Konjic woodcarving is practised by people from different ethnic and religious communities. The craft also connects diaspora households with the region. Its continuity depends on working makers and customers, as well as the preservation of beautiful older furniture.

Zmijanje embroidery decorates women’s clothing and household textiles with deep blue thread and geometric patterns. The technique is associated with villages near Banja Luka. A recognisable local style can travel on a sleeve, a wedding garment or a piece of bedding.

Women traditionally embroider together while singing and talking. Learning happens by watching and practising alongside experienced makers. The gathering combines careful handwork with social life: a sewing session can also be a place to exchange news.

Mostar’s Old Bridge was rebuilt in 2004 after its destruction during the 1990s war. The project drew on detailed study of the earlier structure, materials and techniques. Restoring a crossing also restored a familiar part of the city’s daily routes.

Surviving original bridge material is displayed in a museum, while the reconstruction remains identifiable as a reconstruction. Researchers used documentation and archaeological evidence to guide the work. Visitors can encounter both the rebuilt landmark and pieces that survived its destruction.

Mela’s white ballet shoes are preserved in the War Childhood Museum with her memory of ballet classes in 1994. Her teacher explained that they had been made in Sarajevo before wartime production stopped. The shoes record a child’s learning and a local manufacturing history.

Another contributor, Emir, donated his father’s razor. His father, a teacher, was killed in the Srebrenica genocide; the family kept the object after leaving. An ordinary possession can preserve a person’s memory when war has taken away much else.

The museum uses personal objects in workshops designed for different age groups. Books, letters, photographs, toys and recorded memories become starting points for learning. The evidence allows children’s experiences to enter history alongside treaties and military events.

The first convertible-mark banknotes entered circulation on 22 June 1998, with coins following that December. The currency gradually replaced the mixture of money used during and after the war. New everyday cash was part of rebuilding a shared monetary system.

A ten-mark specimen reproduced by the Central Bank reads “KONVERTIBILNIH MARAKA” and “КОНВЕРТИБИЛНИХ МАРАКА”, both meaning “convertible marks”. The same wording appears in Latin and Cyrillic scripts. This is lettering on a documented banknote, reproduced in a 2017 anniversary publication.

ending.text: The 1995 peace agreement ended the war and reorganised the country without extinguishing its statehood. Bosnia and Herzegovina continued with the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska as its two entities, alongside shared state institutions.
